strengths: The paper addresses a practical NLP question: how many additional labels make a small adapted model competitive with a larger prompted model. A careful empirical answer would be valuable without requiring a new algorithm.

Learning curves spanning small samples to full datasets, additional measurements near crossings, and 100 repetitions for most settings provide substantially more information than endpoint comparisons. The attention to variability is particularly useful.

The appendix supplies model identifiers, prompts, training settings, demonstration-selection procedures, and a source-code link. The limitations transparently disclose the reduced ChatGPT evaluation and restricted task coverage.
weaknesses: Evaluation independence and label accounting are insufficiently established. Section 3 randomly re-splits all labelled data; SST-2 contains related phrases from the same source sentences, creating leakage risks unless splitting respects those groups. Page 5 also describes selecting prompts using 1,000 test examples, while an independent development set and the early-stopping criterion are unspecified. These choices can bias performance and understate the labels required for model selection.

The striking result from instruction-tuning Flan-T5 with only 10 examples lacks an audit of prior target-task and target-data exposure. Flan-T5 already underwent extensive instruction training, and re-splitting benchmark data could place previously encountered examples in evaluation. The paper should establish evaluation disjointness and distinguish additional adaptation labels from prior supervision before generalizing this result to new tasks.

The BoolQ prompt in Table 1 asks whether the passage contains an answer to the question. This is an answerability question, whereas BoolQ requires answering the question itself with yes or no. The mismatch compromises the zero-shot comparison and interpretations involving task difficulty. Task-correct prompts and reporting of truncation and invalid outputs are needed.

The instruction-tuning learning curve confounds available data with actual training exposure. Appendix B fixes training at 150 steps with batch size 4, allowing at most 600 example presentations even when thousands of labels are available. Its flat curve therefore cannot establish that additional labelled data provides little benefit. Similarly, ICL uses only two or four random demonstrations; the retrieval alternative is tested only on Flan-T5/SST-2. Conclusions must reflect these restricted ways of using the annotation budget.

The variance-aware break-even analysis lacks a calibrated reliability criterion. Separation of mean-plus/minus-standard-deviation bands does not establish the 'always better' or guaranteed low failure probability language in Appendix C. Unequal test-set sizes introduce different amounts of evaluation noise, and six ChatGPT repetitions provide much less precise variability estimates than 100 repetitions. Shared evaluation examples and uncertainty estimates for paired differences or outperformance probabilities would better support the claimed 25–200% increases in required labels.

Figure 2 shows unexplained 'random baseline' values near 70 macro-F1 for SST-2 and 60 for MRPC/BoolQ, inconsistent with conventional label-independent chance performance for binary macro-F1. Consequently, claims of below-random performance need correction or justification. The scoring implementation should also specify whether invalid predictions encoded as -1 introduce a third class into the macro average.

The explanations in terms of task complexity and model size exceed the experimental controls: complexity is undefined, and BERT versus RoBERTa also changes pretraining. Three English binary tasks could support a focused Findings contribution, but the evaluation and statistical concerns above require corrected experiments and reanalysis before that recommendation is justified. The existing experimental framework makes next-cycle resubmission a reasonable target.
